text:
The person wants to put their usual grocery order, with potatoes, in the basket again.
Reorder that
Order my usual again
Can I get the same order as last week?
I hope you can send me my usual groceries again.
Same as always, please
Please repeat my last order, the one with the potatoes.
Put everything from my old shopping list in the basket
Could you order everything I got last time? I would be happy with the same thing.

A good night starts with a calm room. Many people use a bedtime routine, a dark room and a dehumidifier so the air does not feel heavy while they sleep. A sleep schedule is what tells the phone when to remind you to go to bed and when to wake you. People change it all the time. They say, wake me at six thirty, or make my alarm ten minutes later on Sundays, or turn off the alarm on holidays. Some people like to talk to the speaker before bed and say, I am going to sleep, turn off the lights. A daily sleep check also shows how long you slept, so you can ask, how did I sleep last night?

Person: Text Maria.
Assistant: Sure. What would you like the message to say?
Person: Tell her the carrots burned, so dinner will be late.
Assistant: Okay. Should I say what time dinner will be?
Person: Make it eight, not seven. It was a fancy recipe and I am starting over.
Assistant: Got it. I will send: The carrots burned, so dinner is at eight instead of seven. Do you want me to send it now?
Person: Yes, send it.
Assistant: Sent to Maria.

The person wants to book a haircut before the salon closes for the holiday.
Book a haircut
Can I get a trim on Friday at ten?
Put me down for Friday, no wait, Saturday
I need my hair cut. I have to look healthy for my interview.
Is there a free slot before you close for the holiday? Actually, make it the morning.
Could you please find me a haircut time on Thursday? The ice on the road is bad, so I will walk and I may be five minutes late.
I would love a trim sometime this week, if you have a spot, and sorry, I meant the week after.

Aoife was nine years old, and today she was baking cookies with her dad in their small kitchen. Outside the window, traffic honked on the busy road, but inside it smelled of butter and sugar. Dad was busy sorting the baking trays, so Aoife talked to the smart speaker on the shelf. "Oven on," she said. The speaker answered, "Heating the oven to one hundred and eighty degrees." Then Aoife said, "Timer, twelve minutes," because the recipe card said the cookies needed twelve minutes. The speaker started the timer and counted it down out loud. When it rang, Aoife and her dad opened the oven. The cookies were golden and soft.

The person wants to move money from one of their own accounts to another.
Move fifty dollars to checking
Transfer half of my savings into my main account
I need more in checking for the winter heating bill, so move two hundred over from savings.
Shift double what I moved last month
My hands are busy stirring the soup, so could you please move some money from savings to checking?
My budget is loose this month, so move only ten dollars.
Send a little less than usual from savings to my card account, please.
Please take a hundred out of my savings and put it into the account I use for rent.

Wiremu looked at the clock and groaned. His friends would arrive in fifty minutes, and the floor was covered with crumbs and one huge puzzle. He picked up the last pieces and dropped them in a box. "Clean the living room," he told his phone, "and make it quick, I have to cook." The robot vacuum woke up and began to roll across the floor. Then Wiremu said, "Also tell me when it is finished." The phone said it would send a message when the vacuum was done. In the kitchen, a delicious smell came from the pot of soup he had started earlier. Thirty-five minutes later the phone buzzed. The living room was clean, and the robot had gone back to its dock. Wiremu smiled and set the table.

Bram was sitting at the kitchen table, stirring his tea. He looked at a drawing his grandson had made, and then at his own gray hair in the window. It was time for a haircut. "Please book me a haircut at Sam's barber shop," he said to the tablet. "Do they open early?" The tablet said the shop opens at nine and that Thursday at ten was free. Bram laughed. "A dozen people are always waiting there on Saturdays, so Thursday is better." He said yes, and the tablet booked the time and set a reminder for Thursday at half past nine. Bram put the drawing on the fridge and finished his tea, pleased that he had not needed to phone anybody.

The night shift had been long, and Sylvie could hardly keep her eyes open when she got home. The morning was humid, and birds were starting to tweet in the trees. A magazine lay on the doorstep, so she picked it up and went inside. She was tired enough to forget things, so she said to the smart lock, "Lock up." The lock clicked, and a calm voice said, "The front door is locked." Sylvie nodded. Then she said, "Garage door?" The voice answered that the garage door was closed, too. Now she could finally go upstairs and sleep. She put the magazine on the table, drew the curtains, and was asleep in a minute.

Person: I want to learn some Portuguese for my trip. Be patient with me, I am slow.
Assistant: Of course. Do you want greetings, food words, or directions?
Person: Not food, I know those already. Greetings and polite words only.
Assistant: Good. Boa tarde means good afternoon, and obrigado means thank you.
Person: Please update my phrase list with those.
Assistant: Which list should I use, your travel list or your hobby list?
Person: Travel list. The hobby list is for my gardening words, so don't touch it.
Assistant: Okay. I updated the travel list with both phrases.

Ella was working at the kitchen table while her son drew with crayons beside her. The kitchen smelled of soup, and she was in a hurry. "Remind me at three to send the article to my editor," she said to her phone. The phone answered, "Okay, reminder set for three o'clock." A moment later Ella remembered the school pickup. "No, wait, make it four," she said. "I will be at the school at three." The phone said, "Changed. I will remind you at four o'clock to send the article to your editor." Ella smiled and went back to stirring the soup, glad that the phone had changed the reminder without any fuss, and that she had one thing less to remember.

Music on a phone or speaker is made of songs, artists and playlists. A playlist is like a blanket of songs you put over a mood, such as a calm one for cooking or a loud one for running. People change music all the time. They say, play something upbeat, skip this song, turn it up a little, or cut the volume in half. If a song has a heavy beat and the baby is sleeping, they say, quieter, please. If they like a song, they say, save this one to my favorites. If they want to hear the same artist again, they say, play more like this. The speaker listens and does what was asked.

Li was driving home on a slow road when he remembered the bread. He had started a loaf in the smart oven before leaving, and it was almost done. He pressed the button on the steering wheel. "Please turn the oven down to one hundred and sixty degrees, because I am stuck in traffic and I do not want the bread to burn before I get home," he said politely. The assistant answered, "The oven is now at one hundred and sixty degrees. Would you like me to keep it warm after the timer ends?" "Yes, please," said Li. When he finally opened the door, the air in the kitchen smelled sweet and warm, and the loaf had a gold crust, just right.

name: scale_recipe
does: Changes the amounts in a recipe for a different number of servings and writes out the new list.
inputs: the recipe (a healthy soup or a tray of chicken drum pieces, say), how many people it feeds now, and how many you want to feed
people say:
- Make this lasagna for twelve people
- Cut the recipe in half, there are only two of us
- How much flour do I need if I double the cookies?
- I want to feed six, not four, can you redo the amounts?
- Turn two cups of rice into enough for a crowd

The person wants to know how far they walked or ran.
How far did I go?
How many miles was my run this morning?
Tell me my distance. No, I mean steps, not distance.
I wish to see how far I walked today.
Was it five kilometres or six? Check my walk.
I came back from the dry trail, so how far was that?
Show me the distance I covered, sorry, I mean last week, not today.
Can you tell me how far I ran, please? Yes, that is what I wish to know.

name: plan_week_meals
does: Picks a dinner for each night of the week in the blink of an eye, so nobody has to wonder what to cook while the family waits downstairs.
inputs: how many people will eat, foods to avoid, and the nights when you are out or eating in the car
people say:
- What should we eat this week?
- Plan dinners for the family, no fish
- I do not want to think about cooking, just pick something
- Give me five easy dinners for Monday to Friday
- We are out on Wednesday, so skip that night

Nikhil came home from class, kicked off one muddy boot by the door and looked in the fridge. He had rice, an onion and two eggs. He was tired and wanted something easy. "Fried rice," he said to his phone. The phone found a recipe and read the first step: cook the rice and let it cool. Nikhil put the rice in a pot. "Next step," he said, and the phone read out that he should chop the onion and fry it. Later, he asked, "How much salt?" and the phone said one small pinch. After dinner, he opened a payment app and paid his roommate back for the eggs. Then he washed the pan and went to bed.

Adebayo came home from the hospital at eight in the morning with sore feet. A new pair of sandals was coming in the mail, and he wanted to know where they were. "Where is my package, and when will it get here?" he asked the phone. The phone opened the tracking page, and the map zoomed in on a small blue truck. "Your package is out for delivery. It is three stops away and should arrive by noon," said the assistant. Adebayo asked, "How far is the driver now?" "About two miles," said the phone. Adebayo thanked it, set an alarm for eleven thirty, and fell asleep on the sofa. At noon the doorbell woke him, and the sandals were at the door.

Emi owned a small flower shop, and tonight she was having a party to celebrate ten years in business. She folded the napkins and moved the tables to the side. Then she wiped her hands and said to the speaker by the till, "Play music." Soft jazz came out of the speaker. Later she said, "A bit louder," and the music got louder, but only a little. Her helper asked what time the guests should come. "Seven o'clock sharp," said Emi. She asked the speaker to remind her at six thirty to put out the snacks. At six thirty it spoke up, and Emi put out the snacks, smiled and opened the door.

Darius had moved to the city only a week before, and he did not speak the language well yet. His neighbour had left a note about the recycling day, and he wanted to talk to her. "Could you please tell me how to say, where do I put the recycling, in Portuguese? I want to ask my neighbour, and I do not want to sound rude," he asked his phone. The phone said the sentence slowly, twice, and wrote it on the screen. Darius repeated it. "Please save that phrase," he added. The phone saved it in his list of phrases. That evening, he knocked on his neighbour's door and said it aloud. She smiled, pointed to the white bin by the gate, and said, "Thursdays."

A neighbourhood works well when people tell each other things. A lost pet notice, a street party or a note about noise are common examples. A notice is for sharing news with everyone nearby, and a chapter of the local community group often runs the message board. People change these notices as things change. They say, my dog was found, take the post down, or the party starts one hour later, or please post it again tomorrow. If the noise is a problem, they ask to send a polite message to the neighbour. People who understand how the board works keep their messages short, with a name, a place and a time. It is a usual way to help each other.

Priya was finishing her work on the tenth floor when she remembered two things. "Remind me to call my mother at six, and to buy milk when I am in town," she told her phone. The phone replied, "I will remind you at six to call your mother, and I will remind you about milk when you get to the town centre." Priya looked out of the high window. The sky was turning orange. At six the phone rang its small bell, and she called her mother from the lift. Later, when she walked into town, the phone buzzed again: buy milk. Priya laughed, went into the shop, and bought two bottles.

Piotr had lived in the city for three days, and the nights were strange. Trams rattled outside, and he could not sleep. He wanted to wake early for his first day at work. "Set an alarm for six," he told his phone. Then he sighed. "No, six thirty. I do not want to be too early." The phone changed the alarm and said, "Alarm set for six thirty." Piotr also asked it to describe how he had slept the night before. The phone said he had slept five hours and woken up twice. "No more coffee late in the day," Piotr said to himself, and he asked the phone to remember that his new diet was no coffee after four o'clock. He turned off the light and slept.

Eun-ji did not like phones, but her grandson played football, and she wanted to know how his team was doing. A truck rumbled by on the street as she picked up the strange little speaker he had given her. "Excuse me, could you please tell me the score of the Eagles game? My grandson is playing today, and I would like to know if they won," she said slowly. The speaker answered at once. "The Eagles won three to one." Eun-ji clapped. "And what place are they in now?" she asked. "They are in second place in the league table," said the speaker. She wrote it on a piece of paper to tell her friends. Maybe this strange little thing was useful after all.

A video meeting is a place where people at different desks can talk and see each other. Before the call, someone writes an agenda, a short list of what to talk about. During the call, people share their screens to show a slide or a document. Many workers design their slides the night before. If you are away from your desk, you can say, mute me, or turn off my camera, or I will be back in five minutes. If the sound is bad, people say, can you share your screen again, or please speak up. Some companies even give staff a discount on headsets, so that voices sound clear. A good meeting ends on time, with a short note of what to do next.

name: parcel_status
does: Finds where a parcel is on its way and tells you the day it should arrive.
inputs: the tracking number from the label; if the label was trimmed off a plain box (say, cold butter from a farm shop), the sender and the date work too
people say:
- Where is my parcel?
- When will the box from my aunt come?
- Has the package from the bakery shipped yet?
- I have been waiting all week for my order
- Is my delivery late?

name: plan_quiet_walk
does: Suggests a walking route of a length you choose, away from noisy roads, and tells you the distance and the time.
inputs: where you start (a place like the old iron bridge works well), how long or how far you want to walk, and whether you need ramps or a lift
people say:
- Find me a walk near here
- I want an hour outside, somewhere not loud
- Plan a three mile route for tomorrow
- Where can I walk with a pushchair?
- Show me a loop that starts and ends at the iron bridge

Person: What's my total?
Assistant: Do you mean the total in your checking account, your savings account, or both?
Person: Not savings. Only the card account. I am in the car, so keep it short.
Assistant: Your card account has nine hundred and forty dollars.
Person: Good. I want to buy a bicycle for my son, and I do not want to spend more than that.
Assistant: I can show your balance, but I can't buy things for you. Would you like a gentle reminder before you pay?
Person: Yes, remind me tonight at eight.
Assistant: Done. I will remind you tonight at eight.

Imran was making lunch for his three kids when the shouting began. They had each put one euro on a football match, and now they wanted to know who won. "Dad, ask who won!" shouted his daughter. Imran wiped his clean hands on a towel and said to the kitchen speaker, "What was the score in the Lions game yesterday?" The speaker answered, "The Lions won two to nothing against the Hawks." Imran frowned. "No, sorry, I mean the Tigers, not the Lions." The speaker said, "The Tigers lost one to two against the Sharks." The kids groaned and cheered together. Imran put a plate in front of each of them, and the shouting turned into eating.

When something in a home breaks, there is usually a simple way to fix it or to book someone who can. A filter in a heater or a fridge needs changing every few months, and many people ask their phone to remind them. A small repair, like a tap upstairs that drips, can be booked with a local shop. People say, find a plumber for Tuesday, or move the repair to Friday, or double check the time with them. They also say, how often does this filter need changing? The point is to keep things working so a small problem does not become a big one. A calendar note and a phone number are the two tools most people use.

name: pick_wash_cycle
does: Chooses the wash cycle and the water temperature for a load of clothes, and tells you what a cycle will cost to run.
inputs: what kind of clothes, their colours, how dirty they are, whose they are (like a sister's wool sweater), and whether you want cold water
people say:
- What setting for my jeans?
- Wash this on cold, I do not want it to shrink
- How much will a hot wash be?
- My sister lent me her silk top, what should I do?
- These towels smell, which cycle is best?

The person wants ideas for a birthday present, such as something to give in a party setting.
Gift ideas, please
What should I get my dad for his birthday?
Give me present ideas and remind me to order on Monday
I keep dragging my feet on a present for my brother, so give me three ideas and set a reminder for Friday.
Find me a gift under twenty dollars with free shipping
Suggest a card and a small gift for my teacher, and tell me when her birthday is.
I would like something for my grandma who has everything. Could you give me a few ideas and save the best one to my list?

Vikram was on a work call when his kids ran into the kitchen. They had zoomed around the house all morning and were hungry. He muted the call and told the coffee machine, "Make a double coffee, please, and make it stronger than yesterday." The machine hummed and filled a big cup. Then he looked at the dishwasher. The screen said it needed its monthly cleaning. "Remind me on Saturday to run the cleaning cycle," he told the speaker. The speaker said, "Reminder set for Saturday." Vikram sipped his coffee, which was twice as strong as normal, and went back to the call, glad that his hands were free.

Ella ran a small bakery shop, and her phone was always almost dead. It was lunchtime, and she was eating a sandwich behind the counter when she squinted at the screen. "I can barely see anything in here," she said to the phone. The phone raised the screen brightness. She still frowned. "These letters are tiny." The phone made the text size larger. A yellow note was stuck to the register, and Ella could read it easily now: order flour. She also noticed the battery was at nine percent. "I am about to lose power," she said, and the phone turned on battery saver mode. Ella smiled and went on eating.

The person wants the assistant to read out their unread emails.
Read my mail
Any new email?
Read my unread emails at quarter to eight
I lie on the couch with my phone nearby, so could you read my new messages out loud?
Tell me who emailed me this morning
Is there anything from the painting class in my inbox?
Could you please go through my inbox at quarter to eight and read anything unread, just the sender and the subject?

name: send_text_later
does: Sends a text message at a time you choose, like a note to your housemate about the dishwasher or an invite to a public event.
inputs: who should get it, what it says, and when to send it; say if you prefer a short or a long message
people say:
- Text Sam at eight tomorrow
- Tell the group chat dinner is at seven, but not until noon
- Message Leo later and remind him about the dishwasher
- Don't send it now, wait until Friday
- Wish my aunt a happy birthday first thing in the morning

Siobhan woke up to a beep from her phone. She rubbed her eyes and saw the words missed call. Her sister had called twice. The TV was still on a news channel from last night, so she turned it down. "Call Anna," she mumbled. The phone began to ring. Anna did not answer, and the phone asked if Siobhan wanted to leave a voicemail. "Yes," she said, and then she said, "Hi Anna, it's me. Call me back." Then she asked the phone, "Any messages?" The phone said she had one voicemail and played it. It was her sister, saying she would make a quick visit on Sunday. Siobhan smiled and went to make tea.

Li was texting three friends when the family trip came up. His mom was planning a holiday by the sea, and the trip would continue for a week. He was excited, because it started the next day. He picked up the phone and typed, "Find a hotel by the beach and book it for two nights." The assistant answered, "There is a hotel on the beach with a room free for two nights. How many guests?" Li typed, "Three, and ask for a room with a sea view." The assistant replied, "Done. The room is booked for three guests, and I have asked for a sea view." Li put the phone back in his silver case and showed his mom the message. She said, "Thank you, that was quick."

Eitan was eighty years old and had earned a quiet evening. He sat in his chair with a book, but the light in the room was too bright for his eyes. He spoke to the smart lamp on the left side of his chair. "Excuse me, would you kindly make the light half as bright? My eyes are tired from reading all day, and I would like to keep reading," he said. The lamp dimmed to half. "Is this better?" it asked. "Yes, thank you," said Eitan. He read for another hour in the soft light. When he got sleepy, he said, "Good night," and the lamp turned off by itself. Eitan smiled and went to bed.

An appointment is a time that is kept for you, like a haircut, a visit to the dentist or a check-up. Shops and clinics have opening hours, and you can only book a time when they are open. When people let the assistant know what they want, they say the kind of visit, the day and the time. They change things often. They say, move my haircut to Friday, make it an hour later, cancel the dentist, or is the salon open on Sunday? Hair salons are busy on Saturdays, so people book early. Most places send a reminder the day before, and you can ask the assistant to remind you an hour earlier too.

Lakshmi had never liked computers, but her grandfather had given her his old laptop. One morning the words on the screen looked tiny, and she was late for a class on video. She typed fast, all in lowercase: make the text biger. The assistant understood and said, "I have increased the text size. Is it better now?" Lakshmi typed, yes thx. Then the assistant said, "I also see that your files have not been saved in a while. Would you like a weekly backup?" She typed, ok do it weekly. The assistant set the backup for every Sunday night. Lakshmi sighed with relief, joined the class, and read every word on the screen.

name: water_plan
does: Tells you when and how much to water each plant, so tomatoes and other tasty things grow well.
inputs: the plant's name, where it sits (a warm window or the shelf by the piano), and the last time it was watered
people say:
- Does my basil need a drink?
- When did I last water the tomatoes?
- The fern by the piano looks dry
- How much water for a big pot?
- Remind me to water the garden every other morning

Cooling keeps a room comfortable when it is hot. An air conditioner blows cold air, and a fan only moves the air around. A waiter in a hot restaurant is glad to see the fan above the tables, and the guests cheer when the room gets cooler. People change cooling with a few simple words. They say, it is too warm in here, make it cooler, turn the fan on, or set it to twenty-two degrees. When a room feels weird, cold in one corner and hot in another, they say, point the air up, or slow the fan down. At night many people say, turn the air off at midnight.

Amelie had just taken a shower, and her glasses were foggy. The house felt hot, and her mother was angry that the air conditioner had been broken all week. Now it was fixed, and Amelie's grandparents were coming to stay. She texted the home assistant on her phone: "start cooling the guest room on the twelfth of March at four pm so it's cold when grandma comes". The assistant answered, "Okay. The air conditioner in the guest room will start at four o'clock on the twelfth of March." Amelie wiped her glasses and read the answer. "Make it twenty-two degrees," she typed. The assistant said it was done. Her mother smiled, and there were no angry words that day.

Living near other people means sharing sounds, streets and sometimes problems. A loud party or a barking dog can ruin a quiet evening. Most people first talk to the neighbour in a kind way, or ask a colleague or a friend who lives nearby what to do. Local groups help with events, lost pets and bad noise. People ask their assistant to find the local events this weekend, to write a polite note about the noise, or to remind them to bring the lost cat poster to the shop. If a note works, they say, stop the reminder. If the noise goes on, they ask, who do I call about it? Being kind and clear usually solves it.

A step counter on a phone or a watch counts how many steps you take. It uses the small movements of your body, so it can be wrong if you push a cart or ride on a bus. Many people also like to know the distance and their pace, which is how long one mile or kilometre takes. People change goals and ask for things by saying, how many steps today, what was my pace on that walk, or make my goal ten thousand steps. If the wind is blowing hard and they want a shorter route, they say, plan a short loop. If a number looks wrong, they say, that count is not correct, please check it.

School work is made of subjects, assignments and due dates. A teacher writes an assignment on the board, and students write it in a notebook or a phone. A due date tells you when to hand it in. People ask for help with these things in different words. They say, when is my science project due, remind me to study on Wednesday, or move the reading to after the break. Before an exam, a student may say, quiz me on the capitals, or read my notes out loud. Even lunch matters: a spicy meal might make a hard day better, and some students put a lunch reminder in their calendar. The aim is to finish work calmly and on time.

Hannah put on her sunglasses and her gardening gloves. A big plant fair was starting in a town a hundred and twenty miles away, and she wanted to buy new roses. "How long will it take to drive to the Green Valley plant fair?" she asked the car. The car looked at the traffic. "It will take about two hours and ten minutes. If you leave now, you will arrive at eleven." Hannah looked at the sky. It was going to be a hot day. "Take the fastest road, please," she said. The car showed the route on the screen and began to give directions. Hannah arrived at eleven, just as the gates opened.

Meal planning means choosing what to eat for the week before you go shopping. You pick dinners, think about diets, and pack lunches ahead. A plan saves time because you do not have to ask what is for dinner every night. Recipes often give amounts in ounces, like eight ounces of pasta for two people. People change plans by saying, make dinner vegetarian tonight, give me a meal that takes only twenty minutes, swap Tuesday and Thursday, or go for cheaper meals this week. They also say, make a shopping list from the plan. When the week goes wrong, they say, we are out on Friday, so skip that one.

Imran was ten, and he had asked for a toy motorcycle for his birthday. The box that arrived was the wrong one: it held a deep blue car, not a motorcycle. He told the tablet, "Send this back and print the label." The tablet opened the shop's return page, picked the order, and chose the reason: wrong item. Then the printer in the hall printed the return label. Imran taped the label to the box and gave it to his dad. "Also order the motorcycle again," he said. The tablet put the right toy in the basket and asked his dad to confirm. Dad pressed yes. A few days later, a small red motorcycle rolled out of a new box.
